contents.html: Digital twin technology enables the creation of electronic representations of real-world entities and the ability to view the states and transitions between states of these entities. This report discusses the concept and purpose of digital twin technology and describes its characteristics, features, functions, and expected operational uses. This report also discusses both traditional and novel cybersecurity challenges presented by digital twin technology as well as trust considerations in the context of existing NIST guidance and documents.
contents.html_ja: デジタルツイン技術により、実世界のエンティティの電子的な表現を作成し、それらのエンティティの状態と状態間の遷移を確認できるようになります。本報告書は、デジタルツイン技術の概念と目的を論じ、その特性、機能、働き、想定される運用上の用途を説明します。また、デジタルツイン技術がもたらす従来型および新たなサイバーセキュリティ上の課題と、信頼に関する考慮事項を、既存の NIST のガイダンスや文書の文脈で論じます。

contents.html: The Information Technology Laboratory (ITL) at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) promotes the U.S. economy and public welfare by providing technical leadership for the Nation’s measurement and standards infrastructure. ITL develops tests, test methods, reference data, proof of concept implementations, and technical analyses to advance the development and productive use of information technology. ITL’s responsibilities include the development of management, administrative, technical, and physical standards and guidelines for the cost-effective security and privacy of other than national security-related information in federal information systems.

contents.html: A digital twin (DT) is an electronic representation of a real-world entity; providing the capability to evaluate this entity. A digital twin can emulate both physical things (e.g., buildings, electronics, living things), and non-physical things (e.g., processes, conceptual models). As with many new information technologies, digital twin technology employs existing foundational technologies and may reflect existing capabilities. It covers what currently exists in modeling and simulation but then casts a broader vision for future capabilities. The full benefits of digital twin technology will require interoperable definitions, tools, and standards as well as early consideration of digital twin cybersecurity and trust. This situation is especially true for nascent standards efforts that seek to define and structure the technology.
contents.html_ja: デジタルツイン（DT）とは、実世界のエンティティの電子的な表現であり、そのエンティティを評価する機能を提供します。デジタルツインは、物理的なもの（たとえば建物、電子機器、生物）も、非物理的なもの（たとえばプロセス、概念モデル）も模倣できます。多くの新しい情報技術と同様に、デジタルツイン技術は既存の基盤技術を用いており、既存の機能を反映している場合があります。現在のモデリングとシミュレーションにすでにあるものを対象としつつ、将来の機能についてのより広いビジョンを描いています。デジタルツイン技術の利点を十分に得るには、相互運用可能な定義、ツール、標準に加えて、デジタルツインのサイバーセキュリティと信頼を早期に考慮することが必要です。この状況は、この技術を定義し構造化しようとする、生まれたばかりの標準化の取り組みにとって特に当てはまります。

contents.html: Elements of digital twin technology have long existed in computers and software that represent entities and simulate dynamic behavior. Now, the maturation of numerous underlying technologies is making it possible to broadly apply simulation and modeling in the form of digital representations and make the technology accessible to a much wider user base. The Internet of Things (IoT) has led to the emergence of small, low-cost, battery-powered sensors that connect over a network and enable massive sensor deployment to a wide variety of objects (e.g., modern buildings may have thousands of sensors). These sensors then provide information that can feed and maintain complex models of those objects. The advances in powerful but low-cost processing and storage enable us to maintain, view, and manipulate these digital replicas without having to use special-purpose or expensive hardware. The recent advances in virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR) have enabled inexpensive visualization of digital twins.
contents.html_ja: デジタルツイン技術の要素は、エンティティを表現して動的な振る舞いをシミュレートするコンピュータやソフトウェアに、以前から存在していました。現在では、数多くの基盤技術が成熟したことで、デジタル表現の形でシミュレーションとモデリングを広く適用し、この技術をはるかに幅広いユーザー層が利用できるようにすることが可能になっています。モノのインターネット（IoT）により、ネットワークを介して接続する小型で低コストのバッテリー駆動のセンサーが登場し、多種多様なオブジェクトへの大規模なセンサーの展開が可能になりました（たとえば、現代の建物には数千個のセンサーがあることもあります）。これらのセンサーが提供する情報は、そうしたオブジェクトの複雑なモデルに入力し、維持するために使えます。強力でありながら低コストの処理能力とストレージの進歩により、専用の高価なハードウェアを使わずに、これらのデジタル複製を維持、閲覧、操作できるようになりました。バーチャルリアリティ（VR）と拡張現実（AR）の最近の進歩により、デジタルツインを安価に可視化できるようになりました。

contents.html: Digital twin technology is also an advancement over existing simulation and modeling because it allows for the real-time monitoring of entities while dynamically updating their digital twins. There is also a trend to remote control physical entities by manipulating dynamic models (i.e., digital twins) as opposed to directly manipulating the objects themselves. Such control is more indirect and abstracts away details that humans may not be able to manage.

contents.html: One approach to establishing standards for digital twin technology is to focus on standard mechanisms for exchanging information, such as the representation of real-world objects. Algorithms that simulate the dynamic behavior of objects could remain proprietary to protect intellectual property, but the description of the object whose behavior is being simulated could be standardized and open in order to be exchanged between applications, domains, industries, and vertical markets. In the simulation and modeling arena, there are many sophisticated software tools and applications that support 2D and 3D modeling and engineering analysis. Each of these applications uses proprietary internal models to represent the objects being modeled (i.e., those created by the user). They also use proprietary and often closely guarded algorithms that represent the functional capabilities for modeling and simulation.
contents.html_ja: デジタルツイン技術の標準を確立する 1 つのアプローチは、実世界のオブジェクトの表現など、情報を交換するための標準的なメカニズムに焦点を当てることです。オブジェクトの動的な振る舞いをシミュレートするアルゴリズムは、知的財産を保護するために独自のままにできますが、振る舞いがシミュレートされるオブジェクトの記述は、アプリケーション、ドメイン、産業、垂直市場の間で交換できるように、標準化して公開できます。シミュレーションとモデリングの分野には、2D および 3D のモデリングや工学的解析を支える高度なソフトウェアツールやアプリケーションが数多くあります。これらのアプリケーションはそれぞれ、モデル化するオブジェクト（すなわちユーザーが作成したもの）を表現するために、独自の内部モデルを使います。また、モデリングとシミュレーションの機能的能力を表す、独自の、多くは厳重に秘匿されたアルゴリズムも使います。

contents.html: Two of the supportive technologies that support the recent interest in digital twin technology are VR/AR and IoT. One expectation for digital twin technology is to leverage VR and AR to create enhanced user interfaces and user experiences for human beings to comprehend the modeling, simulation, monitoring, and command and control of complex entities. Humans rely heavily on visual sensory input, and VR and AR promise to present models of real-world entities through a medium that is amenable to human consumption and comprehension.

contents.html: IoT has been referenced in digital twin discussions and literature thanks to recent advances in sensors and their ongoing and dramatic proliferation in various operations. These sensors are typically network-connected and drive the ability of digital twins to model real-world objects in ways that were not possible until recently. Additionally, IoT devices are often used to create an information fabric or “network” that consists of the observed entities, the sensors that observe and gather information, the connectivity elements, the processing components (i.e., backend compute servers), and the components that use the processed IoT data. With these new sensors being deployed on an IoT fabric, digital twins can represent and dynamically maintain the representation of an instance of an instrumented object [5].
contents.html_ja: IoT は、センサーの最近の進歩と、さまざまな運用におけるセンサーの継続的かつ劇的な普及のおかげで、デジタルツインの議論や文献で言及されてきました。これらのセンサーは通常ネットワークに接続されており、デジタルツインが最近まで不可能だった方法で実世界のオブジェクトをモデル化する能力を支えています。さらに、IoT デバイスは、観測対象のエンティティ、観測して情報を収集するセンサー、接続要素、処理コンポーネント（すなわちバックエンドの計算サーバー）、処理された IoT データを使うコンポーネントから成る、情報ファブリックまたは「ネットワーク」を作り出すためによく使われます。これらの新しいセンサーが IoT ファブリック上に展開されることで、デジタルツインは、計装されたオブジェクトのインスタンスの表現を表し、動的に維持できます [5]。

contents.html: Thus, the application of digital twins goes beyond simply modeling a class of real-world entities. It can also be used to represent and track a specific object, maintain the real-time status, and present a dynamically updated view to a user. With an accurate understanding of the state of an object, a digital twin may also be manipulated by a user to control the actual object, meaning that DT technology may advance beyond traditional modeling and simulation software to encompass command-and-control. For example, operators could remotely command surface rail or subway trains from an operations center.
contents.html_ja: したがって、デジタルツインの応用は、実世界のエンティティのクラスを単純にモデル化することにとどまりません。特定のオブジェクトを表現して追跡し、リアルタイムの状況を維持し、動的に更新された表示をユーザーに提示するためにも使えます。オブジェクトの状態を正確に把握していれば、ユーザーがデジタルツインを操作して実際のオブジェクトを制御することもでき、これは DT 技術が従来のモデリングおよびシミュレーションソフトウェアを超えて、コマンドと制御を包含するようになる可能性があることを意味します。たとえば、オペレーターは運行管制センターから地上の鉄道や地下鉄の列車をリモートでコマンド制御できます。

contents.html: Depending on the object, a system that monitors the object’s state may need to understand the state’s rates of change. Scientists and engineers could create models of real-world conditions and employ them to train AI systems to recognize those conditions. Such applications for simulation, modeling, and monitoring are major motivation for advancing digital twin technology.

contents.html: A digital twin definition is a formal description of the real-world entity that the digital twin represents. For the purposes of this report, think of a formal description as a technical definition of a particular category or class of real-world objects.
contents.html_ja: デジタルツイン定義とは、デジタルツインが表現する実世界のエンティティの形式的な記述です。本報告書では、形式的な記述を、実世界のオブジェクトの特定のカテゴリまたはクラスの技術的な定義と考えてください。

contents.html: The starting point for all activity involving digital twin technology is to create or find a digital twin definition that represents the type of real-world object that is to be represented virtually. Computer software applications are then used to create an instance for that definition to hold and/or maintain the state of the represented object. These digital twin electronic instances can represent both static and dynamic models of the real-world entities that correspond to their respective digital twin definitions.
contents.html_ja: デジタルツイン技術に関わるすべての活動の出発点は、仮想的に表現する実世界のオブジェクトの種類を表すデジタルツイン定義を作成または探すことです。次に、その定義に対するインスタンスを作成し、表現されたオブジェクトの状態を保持または維持するために、コンピュータのソフトウェアアプリケーションを使います。これらのデジタルツインの電子的なインスタンスは、それぞれのデジタルツイン定義に対応する実世界のエンティティの静的モデルと動的モデルの両方を表現できます。

contents.html: The specific digital twin definition created for some object types will dictate the precise makeup of the artifacts that are instantiated from the definition. For example, a digital twin definition is not required to include a dynamic view of its real-world counterpart. Rather, it could comprise only a static view of the object. Thus, not all digital twin definitions will necessarily contain all possible declarations or definition constructs defined in some future standard. Similarly, not all hypertext markup language (HTML) files utilize all tags defined by the HTML standard [6]. If a particular digital twin definition only supports representing a static model of an entity, the related instances would contain no dynamic information, such as how to render animation, video, or dynamic graphics. Consider, for example, a VR presentation of a naval vessel. A static view could represent the internal elements of the ship seen through VR as if a person were literally walking through the vessel. VR technology would be more amenable to this application than a 3D PDF view. The latter would comprise detailed engineering drawings tantamount to an architect’s blueprint drawings. However, it would be difficult to present the equivalent of what a person would see walking through the interior of the ship.
contents.html_ja: あるオブジェクトの種類に対して作成される具体的なデジタルツイン定義が、その定義からインスタンス化される成果物の正確な構成を決定します。たとえば、デジタルツイン定義は、対応する実世界のエンティティの動的な表示を含む必要はありません。むしろ、オブジェクトの静的な表示のみで構成されることもあります。したがって、すべてのデジタルツイン定義が、将来の標準で定義される、可能なあらゆる宣言や定義の構成要素を必ず含むわけではありません。同様に、すべてのハイパーテキストマークアップ言語（HTML）ファイルが、HTML 標準で定義されたすべてのタグを使うわけではありません [6]。特定のデジタルツイン定義がエンティティの静的モデルの表現のみをサポートする場合、関連するインスタンスには、アニメーション、ビデオ、動的なグラフィックスの描画方法といった動的な情報は含まれません。たとえば、艦船の VR プレゼンテーションを考えてみましょう。静的な表示では、人が実際に船内を歩いているかのように、VR を通じて見た船の内部の要素を表現できます。この用途には、3D PDF の表示よりも VR 技術のほうが適しています。後者は、建築家の設計図に相当する詳細な設計図面で構成されます。しかし、船の内部を歩いたときに人が目にするものに相当するものを提示することは困難です。

contents.html: A digital twin definition should create a model of the object it represents, not just a particular view. The model could then be used to present the desired viewpoint of the real-world entity. contents.html: A static digital twin does not describe its corresponding real-world entity’s behavior [11]. This type of view presents a non-changing model of a real-world twin, regardless of the nature of the real-world entity or how that entity may change over time. The real-world entity may not even exist yet as it would occur during the initial design of an object. Such a model would only be suitable for examining the nature of an object at a point in time. For example, a computer numerical control (CNC) milling machine uses a static 3D model to describe the object to be milled. In the aerospace industry, designers or modelers first create what they call a solid model of the component or entity that they are designing. These comprise static 2D or 3D views of a component, such as an aircraft wing or empennage (i.e., tail assembly). A building architect typically creates drawings of a house to be built with various 2D views, such as a site plan, floor plan, and elevation plans. While architects could adopt the practice of creating 3D views, they would be more difficult to read and less useful to building contractors.
contents.html_ja: 静的なデジタルツインは、対応する実世界のエンティティの振る舞いを記述しません [11]。この種の表示は、実世界のエンティティの性質や、そのエンティティが時間とともにどう変化するかにかかわらず、実世界のツインの変化しないモデルを提示します。実世界のエンティティは、オブジェクトの初期設計の際に生じるように、まだ存在すらしていない場合があります。このようなモデルは、ある時点でのオブジェクトの性質を調べるのにのみ適しています。たとえば、コンピュータ数値制御（CNC）フライス盤は、フライス加工する対象のオブジェクトを記述するために、静的な 3D モデルを使います。航空宇宙産業では、設計者やモデラーは、設計している部品やエンティティについて、まずソリッドモデルと呼ばれるものを作成します。これは、航空機の翼や尾部（すなわち尾翼構造）などの部品の静的な 2D または 3D の表示で構成されます。建築家は通常、建設する住宅の図面を、配置図、平面図、立面図などのさまざまな 2D の表示で作成します。建築家が 3D の表示を作成する慣行を採用することもできますが、それらは読み取りにくく、建築請負業者にとって有用性が低くなります。

contents.html: A human user may execute a digital twin instance to model an object’s changes over time and view the dynamic changes to the object. The object may or may not yet exist. A dynamic model presents a simulation of the operation or dynamic behavior of a real-world entity or object, which describes how an object changes as measured via one or more metrics that represent one or more aspects or characteristics of the object [12]. For example, visual updates to graphics can show how the track of a roller coaster bends as a function of applied force from wind loading, the dynamic response of a building during an earthquake, or how an aircraft’s wing flutters or bends under changing loads in flight. An engineer who wants to understand how a milled block changes in malleability, ductility, or tensile strength over time as it is heated at some rate would need a dynamic model that includes a knowledge of thermodynamics, mechanical engineering, and materials engineering. That is, a dynamic model shows more than just the static dimensions, shape, material, or density of an object.

contents.html: The streamed or downloaded content that represents digital twin-based dynamic simulations could consist of pre-captured video, such as an MPEG-encoded video. In that case, the digital twin application software probably creates the standard video from the simulation run. Alternatively, digital twin application software could create declarative-style content to be parsed, comprehended, and manipulated for display by the client receiving the content. This might look something like HTML from an architecture viewpoint. contents.html: With monitoring, sensors on an object send data to a digital twin instance that maintains a model of that object. The system can be local or remote, use wired or wireless connections, and employ any number of transmission media technologies and protocols (e.g., satellites have sensors that perform ground imaging). The data gathered by the sensors can be transmitted to applications that present 3D graphics, VR or AR experiences to users, or data intended for consumption by another computer program. Users can then view and inspect the model and even run virtual tests on the represented object. For example, a VR capability could enable an airline mechanic to view an engine while it is in operation during flight.
contents.html_ja: 監視では、オブジェクト上のセンサーが、そのオブジェクトのモデルを維持するデジタルツインインスタンスにデータを送ります。システムはローカルでもリモートでもよく、有線接続でも無線接続でもよく、任意の数の伝送媒体技術とプロトコルを使えます（たとえば、衛星には地表の撮像を行うセンサーがあります）。センサーが収集したデータは、3DグラフィックスやVRまたはARの体験をユーザーに提示するアプリケーション、または別のコンピュータプログラムが利用するためのデータに送信できます。ユーザーはその後、モデルを閲覧、検査したり、表現されたオブジェクトに対して仮想的なテストを実行したりすることさえできます。たとえば、VR機能により、航空会社の整備士が飛行中に稼働しているエンジンを見ることができるようになります。

contents.html: Real-time links to real-world objects allow for command and control via a digital twin instance. Command and control systems require bidirectional links, and the transmission of information that must be encoded in the digital twin definition upon which the instance is based. The instance can provide a model of an object that is continuously updated with information from sensors and present that model to users (i.e., humans and other computer systems). The users can then provide high-level modifications to the object model, which the instance transforms into specific detailed commands to achieve the desired final state. AI and ML may be needed to achieve this, such as a self-driving car that receives a destination from a human but handles the actual navigation and steering commands.
contents.html_ja: 実世界のオブジェクトへのリアルタイム接続により、デジタルツインインスタンスを介した指揮・制御が可能になります。指揮・制御システムには双方向の接続と、そのインスタンスの基礎となるデジタルツイン定義に符号化しておかなければならない情報の伝送が必要です。インスタンスは、センサーからの情報で継続的に更新されるオブジェクトのモデルを提供し、そのモデルをユーザー（すなわち人間や他のコンピュータシステム）に提示できます。ユーザーはその後、オブジェクトのモデルに高レベルの変更を加えることができ、インスタンスはそれを、望ましい最終状態を達成するための具体的で詳細なコマンドに変換します。これを実現するには AI と ML が必要になる場合があります。たとえば、自動運転車は人間から目的地を受け取りますが、実際のナビゲーションと操舵のコマンドは自ら処理します。

contents.html: Advances in IoT technology have led to the development of a variety of inexpensive and network-connected sensors that can be used to instrument objects. This instrumentation can then feed digital twin instantiations, enabling the modeling of real-world objects and real-time monitoring (and possibly remote control) of many objects to a fine level of granularity. This monitoring will likely be done with inexpensive, network-connected IoT sensors that may produce untrustworthy data or have vulnerabilities, availability issues, or limited computing capacity, network throughput, power, and upgrade potential. Such cybersecurity issues could lead to the inner workings of real-world objects being revealed and possibly controlled via the digital sphere.
contents.html_ja: IoT 技術の進歩により、オブジェクトを計装するために使える、安価でネットワークに接続されたさまざまなセンサーが開発されました。この計装により、デジタルツインのインスタンス化にデータを供給でき、実世界のオブジェクトのモデル化と、多くのオブジェクトの詳細なリアルタイム監視（および場合によってはリモート制御）が可能になります。この監視は、信頼できないデータを生成したり、脆弱性や可用性の問題を抱えたり、計算能力、ネットワークスループット、電力、アップグレードの可能性が限られていたりする可能性のある、安価でネットワークに接続された IoT センサーで行われる可能性が高いといえます。このようなサイバーセキュリティ上の問題により、実世界のオブジェクトの内部の仕組みが明らかになり、デジタル領域を通じて制御される可能性があります。

contents.html: Each sensor or controller is a separate IoT device. The sheer number and distribution of them could inhibit a malicious entity from completely taking control of the instrumented physical object or gaining a sufficiently broad view. However, digital twin technology involves centralizing data and control feeds from the massive instrumentation of an object. This creates great efficiency in simulation, modeling, and control, but it also centralizes sensitive data and control interfaces. If the digital twin is compromised, the attacker has total access to all data about the instrumented object.

contents.html: Similarly, digital twin definitions may be built on top of one another following an object-oriented programming (OOP) model. They may also use an object representation from another digital twin definition to model objects that have some linkage, be it physical or virtual. The manipulation of a digital twin definition representation can then deceive or corrupt related digital twin definitions and other digital systems that consume the digital twin definition’s object representation.

contents.html: The components that make up digital twin technology have traditional cybersecurity challenges as well, particularly in the areas of confidentiality, integrity, availability, maintainability, reliability, and safety. This section reviews some of these needs and the cybersecurity approaches that are commonly used to address them. Many of these techniques also apply to addressing the novel security challenges discussed in the previous sections.
contents.html_ja: デジタルツイン技術を構成するコンポーネントにも、特に機密性、完全性、可用性、保守性、信頼性、安全性の領域で、従来型のサイバーセキュリティ上の課題があります。本節では、これらのニーズの一部と、それらに対処するために一般的に使われるサイバーセキュリティのアプローチを確認します。これらの手法の多くは、前の節で論じた新たなセキュリティ上の課題への対処にも適用されます。

contents.html: Any serious effort to secure a digital twin system should follow more exhaustive risk management guidance, such as the NIST Risk Management Framework (RMF) [20], the NIST Cybersecurity Framework [21], and the NIST Privacy Framework [22]. Additionally, both a digital twin and its instrumentation should have cybersecurity controls implemented and tested to protect against attack using a comprehensive cybersecurity control catalog, such as the previously referenced NIST Cybersecurity Framework [21] or NIST Special Publication (SP) 800-53, Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Info Systems and Organizations [23]. Digital twin technology relies upon IoT cybersecurity for physical objects and instrumentation, and guidance is available through the NIST Cybersecurity for IoT Program [24]. Public and standardized encryption algorithms should be used to ensure the cybersecurity of data in transit from IoT devices to the central digital twin definition repository since proprietary encryption schemes can be weak and lack thorough vetting. Other mechanisms, such as hashes and error detection, should be used to verify the authenticity and integrity of the communications and the data regardless of strong encryption. Such additional protections will enable the system to protect against certain attacks, such as adversary-in-the-middle attacks and support non-repudiation and other services required for certain applications.
contents.html_ja: デジタルツインシステムを保護するための本格的な取り組みは、NIST Risk Management Framework（RMF）[20]、NIST Cybersecurity Framework [21]、NIST Privacy Framework [22]など、より網羅的なリスク管理のガイダンスに従うべきです。さらに、デジタルツインとその計装の両方に、前述のNIST Cybersecurity Framework [21]やNIST Special Publication（SP）800-53, Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Info Systems and Organizations [23]などの包括的なサイバーセキュリティ管理策カタログを用いて、攻撃から保護するためのサイバーセキュリティ管理策を実装し、テストすべきです。デジタルツイン技術は、物理的なオブジェクトと計装のためのIoTサイバーセキュリティに依存しており、NIST Cybersecurity for IoT Program [24]を通じてガイダンスを入手できます。独自の暗号方式は脆弱で、十分な審査を経ていない可能性があるため、IoTデバイスから中央のデジタルツイン定義リポジトリへの転送中のデータのサイバーセキュリティを確保するには、公開された標準化暗号アルゴリズムを使うべきです。強力な暗号化を使うかどうかにかかわらず、通信とデータの真正性と完全性を検証するために、ハッシュやエラー検出などの他のメカニズムを使うべきです。こうした追加の保護により、中間者攻撃（adversary-in-the-middle attack）など特定の攻撃からシステムを保護し、否認防止や、特定のアプリケーションに必要なその他のサービスもサポートできるようになります。

contents.html: A digital twin instance, its current state, and the collected data should be encrypted when not being actively used in order to achieve data at rest cybersecurity. Data governance policies and mechanisms must be in place to ensure that only the correct staff have access to the necessary data within a digital twin instance. Strong authentication mechanisms must then support this governance to ensure that the access policies are not subverted. This can include two-factor or multi-factor authentication as well as the use of hardware keys. The physical security of a digital twin instance and related supportive IT system need to be maintained since physical access is often sufficient to circumvent many digital security mechanisms. This includes both the IoT instrumentation of the monitored object and the hardware maintaining the digital twin instance<sup>4</sup>.
contents.html_ja: 保存データのサイバーセキュリティを実現するために、デジタルツインインスタンス、その現在の状態、収集されたデータは、積極的に使用されていないときは暗号化すべきです。デジタルツインインスタンス内の必要なデータには、適切な担当者のみがアクセスできるようにするため、データガバナンスのポリシーとメカニズムを整備しなければなりません。さらに、アクセスポリシーが覆されないよう、強力な認証メカニズムがこのガバナンスを支えなければなりません。これには、二要素認証や多要素認証、ハードウェアキーの使用が含まれます。物理的なアクセスだけで多くのデジタルセキュリティメカニズムを回避できることが多いため、デジタルツインインスタンスと関連する支援 IT システムの物理的なセキュリティを維持する必要があります。これには、監視対象のオブジェクトの IoT 計装と、デジタルツインインスタンスを維持するハードウェアの両方が含まれます<sup>4</sup>。

contents.html: This section lists a set of 14 trust considerations to help determine whether digital twin technology can provide desired operational functionality with an acceptable level of quality. Trust is the probability that the intended behavior and the actual behavior are equivalent given a fixed context, environment, and point in time. Here, trust is viewed as a level of confidence that a digital twin is functionally equivalent to a physical object, that a specific digital twin can be composed with another digital twin, that enough information is available about the environment and context of the physical object, and that digital twin technology can be standardized to the point where certification of a digital twin is possible.
contents.html_ja: 本節では、デジタルツイン技術が望ましい運用上の機能を許容できる品質で提供できるかどうかを判断するのに役立つ、14 の信頼に関する考慮事項を挙げます。信頼とは、固定された文脈、環境、時点を前提として、意図された振る舞いと実際の振る舞いが等価である確率です。ここでは、信頼は、デジタルツインが物理的なオブジェクトと機能的に等価であること、特定のデジタルツインを別のデジタルツインと組み合わせられること、物理的なオブジェクトの環境と文脈について十分な情報が得られること、デジタルツインの認証が可能なところまでデジタルツイン技術を標準化できることへの確信の度合いとして捉えられます。

contents.html: Digital twin creation ordering: The point in time at which a digital twin is created will affect the correctness of the digital twin, such as whether it is created before the physical object is created or whether it is reverse-engineered from the physical entity that it is intended to mirror. While both approaches are valid, the fidelity of the digital twin may be reduced if it is created after the physical entity exists because there may be internal unknowns about the existing physical entity that cannot be discovered. For example, the source code for commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) software is unavailable to customers or integrators and, thus, hides internal syntax. This is a trust consideration for digital twins.
contents.html_ja: デジタルツインの作成順序: デジタルツインが作成される時点は、デジタルツインの正確さに影響します。たとえば、物理的なオブジェクトが作られる前に作成されるか、模倣することを意図している物理的なエンティティからリバースエンジニアリングされて作成されるかです。どちらの方法も有効ですが、物理的なエンティティが存在した後でデジタルツインを作成すると、既存の物理的なエンティティについて、発見できない内部の未知の部分がある可能性があるため、デジタルツインの忠実度が低下する場合があります。たとえば、市販のオフザシェルフ（COTS）ソフトウェアのソースコードは顧客やインテグレーターには入手できないため、内部の構文が隠されています。これはデジタルツインに関する信頼の考慮事項です。

contents.html: Temporal: Digital twin technology has an implied temporal component to it, particularly since it deals with physical objects that are bound by time. Hardware reliability theory and modeling states that physical objects suffer from levels of decay over time, even when idle. For example, if a car has not been turned on for years, the battery is likely dead, and the car will not start. However, a digital twin will not degrade or fatigue over time. Therefore, at some point, the real-world entity and the digital twin will be in conflict on some level, and synchronization of the two should occur. For example, a metal part could develop hairline fractures after usage that are not represented in the digital twin. This might suggest that the digital twin needs to be reworked or maintained to account for this. For example, a physical object at time \(t+1\) will likely be different than at time \(t\). However, the digital twin should be the same at times \(t\) and \(t+1\) unless it updates dynamically with feeds from the physical object. Having access to an accurate timestamp [26] for the physical object and digital twin is a trust consideration.
contents.html_ja: 時間的側面: デジタルツイン技術には、特に時間に拘束される物理的なオブジェクトを扱うため、暗黙の時間的要素があります。ハードウェアの信頼性理論とモデリングは、物理的なオブジェクトは、使われずにいても、時間とともにある程度劣化すると述べています。たとえば、自動車を何年も動かしていなければ、バッテリーはおそらく上がっていて、エンジンはかからないでしょう。しかし、デジタルツインは時間とともに劣化したり疲労したりしません。したがって、ある時点で、実世界のエンティティとデジタルツインは何らかのレベルで食い違うようになり、両者の同期が行われるべきです。たとえば、金属部品は使用後に、デジタルツインに表現されていないヘアラインのひび割れが生じることがあります。これは、これを考慮してデジタルツインを作り直すか、保守する必要があることを示唆するかもしれません。たとえば、時刻 \(t+1\) における物理的なオブジェクトは、時刻 \(t\) とは異なっている可能性が高くなります。しかし、デジタルツインは、物理的なオブジェクトからのフィードで動的に更新されない限り、時刻 \(t\) と \(t+1\) で同じであるはずです。物理的なオブジェクトとデジタルツインの正確なタイムスタンプ [26] を利用できることは、信頼の考慮事項です。

contents.html: Environment: Digital twin technology has an implied or explicit environmental component that cannot be overlooked. For physical objects, a description of the environmental tolerances or expected usage profiles is needed for many of the “ilities” [27], particularly interoperability. For example, bricks used to construct buildings are made from a variety of materials; some bricks will break easier under stress than others, and some bricks are better suited to certain temperatures and climates. This additional expected operational usage information should be stored with a digital twin. Without it, it will be difficult to determine whether the physical object is “fit for purpose” since purpose implies environment and context. Unknown environmental influences have plagued safety-critical systems and software. Consider PowerPoint running during a presentation. Usually, the presenter does little more than touch the page-up or page-down keys. One could argue that the operational profile for executing PowerPoint during a presentation is two-fold: 1) the loaded presentation and 2) the button inputs from the presenter. However, whether the presentation goes smoothly (e.g., reliably and in a timely manner) is also a function of all of the inputs that PowerPoint is receiving from the disk, memory, and the OS in real time. If, for example, the presentation gets stuck going from slide \(x\) to slide \(x+1\), then something related to “unknown” (i.e., phantom-like) environmental influences is probably involved (e.g., another process running on the machine at the same time and stealing resources and computing cycles). Accurately defining as many environmental factors as possible is a trust consideration.
contents.html_ja: 環境: デジタルツイン技術には、見過ごせない暗黙的または明示的な環境の要素があります。物理的なオブジェクトについては、多くの「イリティ（〜性）」[27]、特に相互運用性のために、環境許容度や想定される使用プロファイルの記述が必要です。たとえば、建物の建設に使われるレンガはさまざまな素材でできています。応力で壊れやすいレンガもあれば、特定の温度や気候により適したレンガもあります。この追加の想定される運用上の使用情報は、デジタルツインとともに保存すべきです。それがなければ、目的には環境と文脈が含まれるため、物理的なオブジェクトが「目的に適合している」かどうかを判断することは困難です。未知の環境の影響は、安全性が極めて重要なシステムやソフトウェアを悩ませてきました。プレゼンテーション中に動作している PowerPoint を考えてみましょう。通常、発表者はページアップキーやページダウンキーに触れる程度のことしかしません。プレゼンテーション中に PowerPoint を実行する際の運用プロファイルは、1) 読み込まれたプレゼンテーションと 2) 発表者のボタン入力の 2 つだ、と主張することもできます。しかし、プレゼンテーションが円滑に進むか（たとえば、確実に、かつ適時に）どうかは、PowerPoint がディスク、メモリ、OS からリアルタイムで受け取るすべての入力の関数でもあります。たとえば、プレゼンテーションがスライド \(x\) からスライド \(x+1\) への移行で止まる場合、おそらく「未知の」（すなわち幽霊のような）環境の影響（たとえば、同時にマシン上で動作して資源や計算サイクルを奪う別のプロセス）に関する何かが関係しているでしょう。できるだけ多くの環境要因を正確に定義することは、信頼の考慮事項です。

contents.html: Manufacturing defects: A digital twin may be used to guide a manufacturing process. For example, a factory that produces light bulbs will have a certain defect rate per thousand bulbs, and the packaging will offer an approximation for how long a bulb will operate before burnout. This highlights that a digital twin could not only describe the underlying components of an average bulb but also suggest how it should be manufactured if the representation details a metric, such as time-to-burnout. Ensuring that a manufacturing process produces a product with the correct life expectancy based on the information in a digital twin is a trust consideration.
contents.html_ja: 製造上の欠陥: デジタルツインは、製造プロセスを導くために使われる場合があります。たとえば、電球を製造する工場には、1,000 個あたり一定の不良率があり、パッケージには電球が切れるまでにどれくらい動作するかのおおよその目安が記載されています。これは、表現が燃え尽きるまでの時間などの指標を詳細に示している場合、デジタルツインが平均的な電球の基本的な構成要素を記述できるだけでなく、どのように製造すべきかも示唆できることを際立たせます。デジタルツインの情報に基づいて、製造プロセスが正しい寿命の製品を生産することを確実にすることは、信頼の考慮事項です。

contents.html: Functional equivalence: Digital twin technology needs a means to determine functional equivalence between the digital twin and the physical object. If the digital twin is an executable specification, then it should produce the same outputs that the physical object produces for the same input data. Otherwise, functional equivalence has not been achieved. This could occur for a variety of factors, such as decay, fatigue, manufacturing variances, or other environmental influences that the physical object experiences during operation but that the digital twin does not. Without some assessment of the level of functional equivalence, it is difficult to argue for trustworthiness.6
contents.html_ja: 機能的等価性: デジタルツイン技術には、デジタルツインと物理的なオブジェクトとの間の機能的等価性を判断する手段が必要です。デジタルツインが実行可能な仕様である場合は、同じ入力データに対して物理的なオブジェクトが生成するのと同じ出力を生成すべきです。そうでなければ、機能的等価性は達成されていません。これは、劣化、疲労、製造上のばらつき、あるいは、物理的なオブジェクトが運用中に経験するがデジタルツインは経験しないその他の環境の影響など、さまざまな要因で生じる可能性があります。機能的等価性のレベルを何らかの形で評価しなければ、信頼性を主張することは困難です。6

contents.html: Composability and complexity: A digital twin that is too complicated can create a composability problem in terms of predicting the trustworthiness of a final composed system from more than one digital twin. Assume that a system has five physical components (i.e., real-world entities), and each component has a corresponding digital twin definition. Physically connecting the five components may be straightforward, but composing the five digital twins may not be, particularly if the digital twins contain information such as tolerances and expected operational usages. Standards can help prune extraneous information contained in a digital twin by defining required interconnects between components of a domain and enabling the composition to be modelled and tested. One approach might be separating classes of information into categories, such as “need to know” and “extraneous.”
contents.html_ja: 構成可能性と複雑性: 複雑すぎるデジタルツインは、複数のデジタルツインから構成される最終的なシステムの信頼性を予測するうえで、構成可能性の問題を引き起こす可能性があります。システムに 5 つの物理的なコンポーネント（すなわち実世界のエンティティ）があり、各コンポーネントに対応するデジタルツイン定義があると仮定します。5 つのコンポーネントを物理的に接続することは簡単かもしれませんが、5 つのデジタルツインを構成することは、特にデジタルツインに許容度や想定される運用上の使用といった情報が含まれている場合は、簡単でないかもしれません。標準は、ドメインのコンポーネント間で必要な相互接続を定義し、構成をモデル化してテストできるようにすることで、デジタルツインに含まれる余分な情報を取り除くのに役立ちます。1 つのアプローチは、情報のクラスを「知る必要のあるもの」と「余分なもの」などのカテゴリーに分けることです。

contents.html: Instrumentation and monitoring: Instrumentation of a digital twin is a beneficial and unique advantage that digital twin technology offers. While one might not be able to instrument the physical object, one may be able to instrument the digital twin. However, instrumentation and probes are not as simple or easy to correctly inject into a digital twin as might be expected. Much can be learned here from the safety-critical software community. First, a determination of where to inject the probes is necessary [28], though this is not easy and can be more art than science. Second, the number of probes to inject is also a consideration. As shown in real-time systems, probes can slow down performance and timing, which may cause a problem for synchronization between the digital twin and physical object. That said, there are ways to reduce this impact by having the probes only collect raw data rather than compute internal test results, such as built-in self-tests. Collecting the “right” information from the internal state of an executing digital twin is an expensive and error-prone effort.
contents.html_ja: 計装と監視: デジタルツインの計装は、デジタルツイン技術が提供する有益で独特な利点です。物理的なオブジェクトを計装できなくても、デジタルツインを計装できる場合があります。しかし、計装とプローブは、想定されるほど単純でも、デジタルツインに正しく挿入するのが容易でもありません。ここでは、安全性が極めて重要なソフトウェアのコミュニティから多くを学べます。第一に、プローブをどこに挿入するかの判断が必要ですが [28]、これは容易ではなく、科学というより技の領域になりえます。第二に、挿入するプローブの数も考慮事項です。リアルタイムシステムで示されているように、プローブは性能とタイミングを遅くする可能性があり、デジタルツインと物理的なオブジェクトの同期に問題を引き起こす場合があります。とはいえ、プローブに、組み込み自己テストのような内部のテスト結果を計算させるのではなく、生データだけを収集させることで、この影響を減らす方法があります。実行中のデジタルツインの内部状態から「適切な」情報を収集することは、費用がかかり、エラーが起きやすい作業です。

contents.html: Heterogeneity of standards: Heterogeneity of different formats for digital twins may cause composability problems [29]. Composing digital twin definitions from different component vendors may not be achievable if vendors misuse standardized formats [4]. This is a consideration for trusting composed digital twins.
contents.html_ja: 標準の異質性: デジタルツインの異なる形式の異質性が、構成可能性の問題を引き起こす場合があります [29]。ベンダーが標準化された形式を誤用すると、異なるコンポーネントベンダーのデジタルツイン定義を組み合わせることができない場合があります [4]。これは、組み合わせたデジタルツインを信頼するための考慮事項です。

contents.html: Non-functional requirements: Functional requirements state what a system shall do, negative requirements state what a system shall not do, and non-functional requirements (i.e., the “ilities”7) typically state what level of quality the system shall exhibit for both the functional and negative requirements. The “ilities” apply to both “things” and the systems into which they are built. The issue for digital twin technology concerns how many of the non-functional requirements can be written for the functional and negative requirements, thus defining the level of quality for what the system should and should not do. The ability to write these non-functional requirements will affect the ability to claim the trustworthiness of a composite object.
contents.html_ja: 非機能要件: 機能要件はシステムが何をしなければならないかを述べ、否定的要件はシステムが何をしてはならないかを述べます。非機能要件（すなわち「イリティ（〜性）」7）は通常、機能要件と否定的要件の両方について、システムが示さなければならない品質の水準を述べます。「イリティ」は、「もの」と、それが組み込まれるシステムの両方に適用されます。デジタルツイン技術における課題は、機能要件と否定的要件について非機能要件をどれだけ記述できるか、ひいてはシステムがすべきこととすべきでないことの品質水準を定義できるかという点です。これらの非機能要件を記述する能力は、複合オブジェクトの信頼性を主張できるかどうかに影響します。

contents.html: Digital twin accuracy: The degree to which the digital twin is correct is a trust consideration that may benefit from having more than one independently created digital twin for a specific physical object. In n-version programming [30], more than one independent software implementation is created for highly critical systems that the software impacts because no single implementation can be assumed to be adequately trustworthy. Each independent implementation is run in parallel, and the outputs from each implementation are sent to a voter that then decides on the final output that the system receives.
contents.html_ja: デジタルツインの正確さ: デジタルツインがどの程度正しいかは信頼の考慮事項であり、特定の物理的なオブジェクトに対して独立に作成された複数のデジタルツインを用意することが有益な場合があります。N バージョンプログラミング [30] では、ソフトウェアが影響を及ぼす非常に重要なシステムのために、単一の実装では十分に信頼できると仮定できないことから、独立した複数のソフトウェア実装が作成されます。独立した各実装は並列に実行され、各実装の出力は投票器に送られ、投票器がシステムが受け取る最終的な出力を決定します。

contents.html: Testing: The testability of a digital twin refers to measuring how likely an error or defect will be detected during testing. Systems that are less likely to reveal the presence of defects are deemed less testable. Physical objects are testable to different degrees using this definition, though the methods for testing digital twins that are most likely to demonstrate that the digital representation is correct are unclear. One option is to ignore this trust consideration and decide that a digital twin is untestable and, therefore, stands alone as the “oracle” or “gold standard.” Moreover, although testing usually involves expected use cases, cases of misuse should also be considered.
contents.html_ja: テスト: デジタルツインのテスト容易性とは、テスト中にエラーや欠陥が検出される可能性の高さを測ることを指します。欠陥の存在を明らかにする可能性が低いシステムは、テスト容易性が低いと見なされます。この定義を使うと、物理的なオブジェクトはさまざまな程度でテスト可能ですが、デジタル表現が正しいことを示す可能性が最も高いデジタルツインのテスト方法は明確ではありません。1 つの選択肢は、この信頼の考慮事項を無視し、デジタルツインはテスト不可能であり、したがって「オラクル」または「ゴールドスタンダード」として独立していると判断することです。さらに、テストは通常、想定される使用ケースを対象としますが、誤用のケースも考慮すべきです。

contents.html: Certification: Certification usually occurs by certifying either the process used to develop or the final artifact that comes from that process [31]. These two types of certification are distinct [3][32][33][34][36][37]. For digital twin technology, this means that one could attempt to certify how the digital twin was created or certify the accuracy of the digital twin itself. Certification of a twin will be complicated by information overload. For example, most prescription drugs come with warnings about who can take them, disclaimers about negative side effects, and when to discontinue use. However, the vast amount of information known about a drug and the vaster amount of unknown information about a drug at time \(t\) will not be known until time \(t+1\), and much of this vital information is only understandable by medical experts. The trust consideration for digital twin technology is how much information can be provided in a specific digital twin without overloading a user with extraneous information that leads to confusion about how to use the twin or what the twin even represents.
contents.html_ja: 認証: 認証は通常、開発に使われたプロセス、またはそのプロセスから生じる最終成果物のいずれかを認証することで行われます [31]。これら 2 種類の認証は別個のものです [3][32][33][34][36][37]。デジタルツイン技術では、これは、デジタルツインがどのように作成されたかを認証しようとすることも、デジタルツイン自体の正確さを認証しようとすることもできることを意味します。ツインの認証は、情報過多によって複雑になります。たとえば、ほとんどの処方薬には、誰が服用できるか、副作用についての免責、服用を中止すべき場合についての警告が付いています。しかし、薬について知られている膨大な情報と、時刻 \(t\) においてその薬について未知のさらに膨大な情報は、時刻 \(t+1\) になるまでわからず、この重要な情報の多くは医療の専門家にしか理解できません。デジタルツイン技術における信頼の考慮事項は、ツインの使い方やツインが何を表しているかについての混乱を招く余分な情報でユーザーに過剰な負担をかけずに、特定のデジタルツインでどれだけの情報を提供できるかです。

contents.html: Propagation: One of the greatest trust concerns with any system of systems is how errors and corrupt data propagate during execution [38]. Digital twin technology experiences this trust consideration as well, particularly when different twins representing different physical objects are composed. This may suggest that a digital twin should be wrapped with pre-conditions and post-conditions to determine whether the output from one digital twin will be acceptable as input to another digital twin.
contents.html_ja: 伝搬: システムのシステムにおける最大の信頼上の懸念の 1 つは、実行中にエラーや破損したデータがどのように伝搬するかです [38]。デジタルツイン技術も、特に異なる物理的なオブジェクトを表す異なるツインを組み合わせる場合に、この信頼の考慮事項に直面します。これは、あるデジタルツインの出力が別のデジタルツインの入力として許容できるかどうかを判断するために、デジタルツインを事前条件と事後条件で包むべきであることを示唆する場合があります。

contents.html: Counterfeiting: A digital twin could be tampered with or counterfeited, and there are schemes that could protect against this. For example, digital twin definitions could be hashed and the hash posted to a public web page, or users of a digital twin definition could hash their copy and compare it to the hash on the public web page. This said, web pages and other similar publicly accessible repositories can be hacked. To enhance trust, one could use a blockchain to publicly post a digital twin definition hash in an immutable data structure that could never be changed, even by malicious attackers. Alternatively, identical copies of a digital twin definitions and related instances could be stored in separate locations (e.g., in offline backups).
contents.html_ja: 偽造: デジタルツインは改ざんまたは偽造される可能性があり、それを防ぐ方式があります。たとえば、デジタルツイン定義のハッシュを計算して公開ウェブページに掲載したり、デジタルツイン定義のユーザーが自分のコピーのハッシュを計算して公開ウェブページ上のハッシュと比較したりできます。とはいえ、ウェブページや同様の公開リポジトリはハッキングされる可能性があります。信頼性を高めるため、ブロックチェーンを使って、悪意ある攻撃者でさえ変更できない不変のデータ構造にデジタルツイン定義のハッシュを公開できます。あるいは、デジタルツイン定義と関連するインスタンスの同一のコピーを別々の場所（たとえばオフラインバックアップ）に保存できます。

contents.html: Digital twin technology is an emerging area of research and standardization, though its core elements of modeling and simulation are already mature and widely used. Other significant components, such as VR, are also frequently deployed (even as low-cost gaming units in homes), and IoT sensors are becoming commonplace. Because of this, there may be a lack of clarity as to what is new with digital twin technology and the promise it holds.
contents.html_ja: デジタルツイン技術は、研究と標準化の新興分野ですが、その中核要素であるモデリングとシミュレーションはすでに成熟し、広く使われています。VR などの他の重要なコンポーネントも頻繁に導入されており（家庭向けの低価格ゲーム機としてさえ）、IoT センサーも一般的になりつつあります。このため、デジタルツイン技術で何が新しいのか、その技術が何を約束するのかが明確でない場合があります。

contents.html: This work discusses the characteristics and underlying technology for digital twin, the motivation and vision for its use, common low-level operations, usage scenarios, and example use cases. It also discussed technical considerations for the cybersecurity and trust of digital twin technology by analyzing both traditional and novel cybersecurity challenges. Furthermore, this work evaluated 14 trust considerations for digital twin functionality and quality and mapped those evaluations to other NIST cybersecurity guidance.
contents.html_ja: 本書は、デジタルツインの特性と基盤技術、その使用の動機とビジョン、一般的な下位レベルの操作、利用シナリオ、ユースケースの例を論じました。また、従来型と新たなサイバーセキュリティ上の課題の両方を分析することで、デジタルツイン技術のサイバーセキュリティと信頼に関する技術的な考慮事項も論じました。さらに、デジタルツインの機能と品質に関する 14 の信頼の考慮事項を評価し、それらの評価を他の NIST のサイバーセキュリティガイダンスに対応づけました。

Digital twin technology enables the creation of electronic representations of real-world entities and the ability to view the states and transitions between states of these entities. This report discusses the concept and purpose of digital twin technology and describes its characteristics, features, functions, and expected operational uses. This report also discusses both traditional and novel cybersecurity challenges presented by digital twin technology as well as trust considerations in the context of existing NIST guidance and documents.

The Information Technology Laboratory (ITL) at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) promotes the U.S. economy and public welfare by providing technical leadership for the Nation’s measurement and standards infrastructure. ITL develops tests, test methods, reference data, proof of concept implementations, and technical analyses to advance the development and productive use of information technology. ITL’s responsibilities include the development of management, administrative, technical, and physical standards and guidelines for the cost-effective security and privacy of other than national security-related information in federal information systems.

This publication is intended for anyone who wants to understand the underlying technology and envisioned capabilities of digital twin technology. It is particularly applicable to Standards Developing Organizations (SDOs) and implementers of digital twin technology.

original_blocks.html: A simplified definition for digital twins1 could be:
A digital twin is the virtual (i.e., digital) representation of a physical or perceived real-world entity, concept, or notion.
A related important term is that of a digital twin definition:
A digital twin definition is a machine-readable specification that describes features that may be modeled for a particular type of real-world entity.

Thus, a digital twin definition refers to a particular type of entity rather than the specific entity itself. It defines the features of an entity type that can be statically and dynamically modeled, how those features will be digitally encoded and represented, and how they will persist in a digital computer environment. Computer software applications will read digital twin definitions to create digital twin instances (or simply, digital twin), which are instantiations of real-world objects that model the state of represented objects.

While many of these real-world entities have physical forms (e.g., an aircraft engine, an oil derrick, a valve in an oil pipeline pumping station), digital twins can also represent something abstract. The DTC definition contains the word “processes,” which is an abstract notion, and the simplified definition discusses entities that may be perceived or conceived without having a physical form. For example, a process in a computer operating system is real, even if it does not have a concrete or physical shape. It is a conglomeration of multiple intangible things, such as electrical signals, the states of registers that contain voltage and current levels, and the electrical state of memory. Whether it is viewed statically or dynamically, a computer program is real, and one can clearly observe the effects that it has on other objects.

1 Section 3 discusses the differences between digital twin technology and traditional modeling and simulation, and Sec. 9 discusses the importance of synchronization between a digital twin and a real-world entity.

IoT has been referenced in digital twin discussions and literature thanks to recent advances in sensors and their ongoing and dramatic proliferation in various operations. These sensors are typically network-connected and drive the ability of digital twins to model real-world objects in ways that were not possible until recently. Additionally, IoT devices are often used to create an information fabric or “network” that consists of the observed entities, the sensors that observe and gather information, the connectivity elements, the processing components (i.e., backend compute servers), and the components that use the processed IoT data. With these new sensors being deployed on an IoT fabric, digital twins can represent and dynamically maintain the representation of an instance of an instrumented object [5].

A digital twin definition should create a model of the object it represents, not just a particular view. The model could then be used to present the desired viewpoint of the real-world entity. A definition can contain as much or as little information about its real-world counterpart as its author desires, which may limit the types of views that can be created. Digital twin definition authors decide the breadth, scope, degree of granularity, and detail.

It is envisioned that there will be many digital twin definitions that describe many kinds of entities. This section also discusses operations on digital twins,2 which are specific instances created from digital twin definitions.

A digital twin definition is a formal description of the real-world entity that the digital twin represents. For the purposes of this report, think of a formal description as a technical definition of a particular category or class of real-world objects.
2 A reference to a “digital twin” without other qualifiers refers to the digital twin instance that represents the entity.

Like existing commercial applications, any future digital twin standard should include a language for describing and defining a digital twin, including formal grammar, syntax, and semantics. It would have to be comprehensive enough to support the definition of artifacts to represent any arbitrary real-world entity that a digital twin can represent [5]. Most likely, a standard would accommodate the creation of static and dynamic 2D, 3D, VR, and AR models for visual presentation to human users. It may also accommodate the creation, manipulation, and persistence of presentation forms that are intended for machine rather than human consumption.

A static digital twin does not describe its corresponding real-world entity’s behavior [11]. This type of view presents a non-changing model of a real-world twin, regardless of the nature of the real-world entity or how that entity may change over time. The real-world entity may not even exist yet as it would occur during the initial design of an object. Such a model would only be suitable for examining the nature of an object at a point in time. For example, a computer numerical control (CNC) milling machine uses a static 3D model to describe the object to be milled. In the aerospace industry, designers or modelers first create what they call a solid model of the component or entity that they are designing. These comprise static 2D or 3D views of a component, such as an aircraft wing or empennage (i.e., tail assembly). A building architect typically creates drawings of a house to be built with various 2D views, such as a site plan, floor plan, and elevation plans. While architects could adopt the practice of creating 3D views, they would be more difficult to read and less useful to building contractors.

A human user may execute a digital twin instance to model an object’s changes over time and view the dynamic changes to the object. The object may or may not yet exist. A dynamic model presents a simulation of the operation or dynamic behavior of a real-world entity or object, which describes how an object changes as measured via one or more metrics that represent one or more aspects or characteristics of the object [12]. For example, visual updates to graphics can show how the track of a roller coaster bends as a function of applied force from wind loading, the dynamic response of a building during an earthquake, or how an aircraft’s wing flutters or bends under changing loads in flight. An engineer who wants to understand how a milled block changes in malleability, ductility, or tensile strength over time as it is heated at some rate would need a dynamic model that includes a knowledge of thermodynamics, mechanical engineering, and materials engineering. That is, a dynamic model shows more than just the static dimensions, shape, material, or density of an object.

The imperative and declarative programming paradigms are both important for the kinds of software applications that will use digital twin technology. Think of the MIT X Window System,3 which represents the imperative programming paradigm to display graphics [15]. Applications make calls to X library routines and those of the graphics toolkits that are built on top of the venerable and X Window System libraries. Those calls draw the graphics, and the X
Xlib Xt
display server renders the visual graphics on the graphics display [16].

In the declarative programming paradigm, the information encoded indicates what is to be displayed rather than how to do it [17]. There are no imperative calls to execute the steps to display the graphics. HTML is an example of a declarative programming paradigm. An HTML file represents directives of what to display, not how to display it. Therefore, there are no imperative commands to display the content like the programmatic calls to routines in the X Window System libraries.

The streamed or downloaded content that represents digital twin-based dynamic simulations could consist of pre-captured video, such as an MPEG-encoded video. In that case, the digital twin application software probably creates the standard video from the simulation run. Alternatively, digital twin application software could create declarative-style content to be parsed, comprehended, and manipulated for display by the client receiving the content. This might look something like HTML from an architecture viewpoint. The content would consist of a combination of declarative constructs, including some that point to other content such as pre-recorded video or even executable code that is in the imperative style. Web pages today contain directives to download and run code, such as JavaScript programs.
3 See https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/X_Window_System.

Unmanned aerial vehicles (drones): Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) or drones are used in environmental monitoring. UAVs come in all sizes, shapes, configurations, and levels of sophistication. More advanced drones can operate autonomously or under the control of a human in a command-and-control center that is far from the UAV’s physical location. Remote operators of UAVs have user interfaces that provide the real-time information about the UAV’s state and condition.

Ocean-going vessels: Digital twins can be used to construct 2D and 3D static views or VR/AR views of ocean vessels. VR/AR views would enable architects, designers, engineers, and maintenance crews to see the vessel as if they were physically walking through it. During operations, digital twin technology would enable operators and crew members to monitor every aspect of the ship, possibly precluding the need for certain physical monitoring and inspections.

Oil derricks and ocean-drilling platforms: Oil derricks may drill for oil in inhospitable and potentially treacherous environments at great depths. Systems built around digital twins enable designers, engineers, and operators to form models and visual representations of oil rigs, drill rigs, and drill bit heads deep in the ocean.

Robotic surgery: There are surgical robots that perform various kinds of surgery. Some require an actual human surgeon to control the robot, while others only require a human surgeon to monitor the robot’s automatic execution of the surgery. Digital twin technology could be used in pre-surgery planning and to foster surgical tool interoperability. For example, one company’s surgical robot could interoperate with another company’s VR system that specializes in the representation of human organs.

Any serious effort to secure a digital twin system should follow more exhaustive risk management guidance, such as the NIST Risk Management Framework (RMF) [20], the NIST Cybersecurity Framework [21], and the NIST Privacy Framework [22]. Additionally, both a digital twin and its instrumentation should have cybersecurity controls implemented and tested to protect against attack using a comprehensive cybersecurity control catalog, such as the previously referenced NIST Cybersecurity Framework [21] or NIST Special Publication (SP) 800-53, Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Info Systems and Organizations [23]. Digital twin technology relies upon IoT cybersecurity for physical objects and instrumentation, and guidance is available through the NIST Cybersecurity for IoT Program [24]. Public and standardized encryption algorithms should be used to ensure the cybersecurity of data in transit from IoT devices to the central digital twin definition repository since proprietary encryption schemes can be weak and lack thorough vetting. Other mechanisms, such as hashes and error detection, should be used to verify the authenticity and integrity of the communications and the data regardless of strong encryption. Such additional protections will enable the system to protect against certain attacks, such as adversary-in-the-middle attacks and support non-repudiation and other services required for certain applications.

A digital twin instance, its current state, and the collected data should be encrypted when not being actively used in order to achieve data at rest cybersecurity. Data governance policies and mechanisms must be in place to ensure that only the correct staff have access to the necessary data within a digital twin instance. Strong authentication mechanisms must then support this governance to ensure that the access policies are not subverted. This can include two-factor or multi-factor authentication as well as the use of hardware keys. The physical security of a digital twin instance and related supportive IT system need to be maintained since physical access is often sufficient to circumvent many digital security mechanisms. This includes both the IoT instrumentation of the monitored object and the hardware maintaining the digital twin instance4.

4 An appropriate architecture for securing aggregated data from disparate databases with different access policies is discussed in DeFranco, J. F., Ferraiolo, D. F., Kuhn, R., & Roberts, J. (2021). A trusted federated system to share granular data among disparate database resources. Computer, 54(3), 55-62.
8. Trust Considerations5

Digital twin creation ordering: The point in time at which a digital twin is created will affect the correctness of the digital twin, such as whether it is created before the physical object is created or whether it is reverse-engineered from the physical entity that it is intended to mirror. While both approaches are valid, the fidelity of the digital twin may be reduced if it is created after the physical entity exists because there may be internal unknowns about the existing physical entity that cannot be discovered. For example, the source code for commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) software is unavailable to customers or integrators and, thus, hides internal syntax. This is a trust consideration for digital twins.

Temporal: Digital twin technology has an implied temporal component to it, particularly since it deals with physical objects that are bound by time. Hardware reliability theory and modeling states that physical objects suffer from levels of decay over time, even when idle. For example, if a car has not been turned on for years, the battery is likely dead, and the car will not start. However, a digital twin will not degrade or fatigue over time. Therefore, at some point, the real-world entity and the digital twin will be in conflict on some level, and synchronization of the two should occur. For example, a metal part could develop hairline fractures after usage that are not represented in the digital twin. This might suggest that the digital twin needs to be reworked or maintained to account for this. For example, a physical object at time t+1 will likely be different than at time t. However, the digital twin should be the same at times t and t+1 unless it updates dynamically with feeds from the physical object. Having access to an accurate timestamp [26] for the physical object and digital twin is a trust consideration.

Environment: Digital twin technology has an implied or explicit environmental component that cannot be overlooked. For physical objects, a description of the environmental tolerances or expected usage profiles is needed for many of the “ilities” [27], particularly interoperability. For example, bricks used to construct buildings are made from a variety of materials; some bricks will break easier under stress than others, and some bricks are better suited to certain temperatures and climates. This additional expected operational usage information should be stored with a digital twin. Without it, it will be difficult to determine whether the physical object is “fit for purpose” since purpose implies environment and context. Unknown environmental influences have plagued safety-critical systems and software. Consider PowerPoint running during a presentation. Usually, the presenter does little more than touch the page-up or page-down keys. One could argue that the operational profile for executing PowerPoint during a presentation is two-fold: 1) the loaded presentation and 2) the button inputs from the presenter. However, whether the presentation goes smoothly (e.g., reliably and in a timely manner) is also a function of all of the inputs that PowerPoint is receiving from the disk, memory, and the OS in real time. If, for example, the presentation gets stuck going from slide x to slide x+1, then something related to “unknown” (i.e., phantom-like) environmental influences is probably involved (e.g., another process running on the machine at the same time and stealing resources and computing cycles). Accurately defining as many environmental factors as possible is a trust consideration.
5 An earlier version of these concerns, based on the draft of this NIST IR, appeared in P. Laplante, "Trusting Digital Twins." Computer 55.7 (2022): 73-77.

Manufacturing defects: A digital twin may be used to guide a manufacturing process. For example, a factory that produces light bulbs will have a certain defect rate per thousand bulbs, and the packaging will offer an approximation for how long a bulb will operate before burnout. This highlights that a digital twin could not only describe the underlying components of an average bulb but also suggest how it should be manufactured if the representation details a metric, such as time-to-burnout. Ensuring that a manufacturing process produces a product with the correct life expectancy based on the information in a digital twin is a trust consideration.

Functional equivalence: Digital twin technology needs a means to determine functional equivalence between the digital twin and the physical object. If the digital twin is an executable specification, then it should produce the same outputs that the physical object produces for the same input data. Otherwise, functional equivalence has not been achieved. This could occur for a variety of factors, such as decay, fatigue, manufacturing variances, or other environmental influences that the physical object experiences during operation but that the digital twin does not. Without some assessment of the level of functional equivalence, it is difficult to argue for trustworthiness.6

Composability and complexity: A digital twin that is too complicated can create a composability problem in terms of predicting the trustworthiness of a final composed system from more than one digital twin. Assume that a system has five physical components (i.e., real-world entities), and each component has a corresponding digital twin definition. Physically connecting the five components may be straightforward, but composing the five digital twins may not be, particularly if the digital twins contain information such as tolerances and expected operational usages. Standards can help prune extraneous information contained in a digital twin by defining required interconnects between components of a domain and enabling the composition to be modelled and tested. One approach might be separating classes of information into categories, such as “need to know” and “extraneous.”
6 Verification and validation can be used to provide evidence of functional equivalence.

Instrumentation and monitoring: Instrumentation of a digital twin is a beneficial and unique advantage that digital twin technology offers. While one might not be able to instrument the physical object, one may be able to instrument the digital twin. However, instrumentation and probes are not as simple or easy to correctly inject into a digital twin as might be expected. Much can be learned here from the safety-critical software community. First, a determination of where to inject the probes is necessary [28], though this is not easy and can be more art than science. Second, the number of probes to inject is also a consideration. As shown in real-time systems, probes can slow down performance and timing, which may cause a problem for synchronization between the digital twin and physical object. That said, there are ways to reduce this impact by having the probes only collect raw data rather than compute internal test results, such as built-in self-tests. Collecting the “right” information from the internal state of an executing digital twin is an expensive and error-prone effort.

Heterogeneity of standards: Heterogeneity of different formats for digital twins may cause composability problems [29]. Composing digital twin definitions from different component vendors may not be achievable if vendors misuse standardized formats [4]. This is a consideration for trusting composed digital twins.

Digital twin accuracy: The degree to which the digital twin is correct is a trust consideration that may benefit from having more than one independently created digital twin for a specific physical object. In n-version programming [30], more than one independent software implementation is created for highly critical systems that the software impacts because no single implementation can be assumed to be adequately trustworthy. Each independent implementation is run in parallel, and the outputs from each implementation are sent to a voter that then decides on the final output that the system receives.

Non-functional requirements: Functional requirements state what a system shall do, negative requirements state what a system shall not do, and non-functional requirements (i.e., the “ilities”7) typically state what level of quality the system shall exhibit for both the functional and negative requirements. The “ilities” apply to both “things” and the systems into which they are built. The issue for digital twin technology concerns how many of the non-functional requirements can be written for the functional and negative requirements, thus defining the level of quality for what the system should and should not do. The ability to write these non-functional requirements will affect the ability to claim the trustworthiness of a composite object.

Testing: The testability of a digital twin refers to measuring how likely an error or defect will be detected during testing. Systems that are less likely to reveal the presence of defects are deemed less testable. Physical objects are testable to different degrees using this definition, though the methods for testing digital twins that are most likely to demonstrate that the digital representation is correct are unclear. One option is to ignore this trust consideration and decide that a digital twin is untestable and, therefore, stands alone as the “oracle” or “gold standard.” Moreover, although testing usually involves expected use cases, cases of misuse should also be considered.

7 Examples of “ilities” include availability, composability, compatibility, dependability, discoverability, durability, fault tolerance, flexibility, interoperability, insurability, liability, maintainability, observability, privacy, performance, portability, predictability, probability of failure, readability, reliability, resilience, reachability, safety, scalability, cybersecurity, sustainability, testability, traceability, usability, visibility, and vulnerability [27].

Certification: Certification usually occurs by certifying either the process used to develop or the final artifact that comes from that process [31]. These two types of certification are distinct [3][32][33][34][36][37]. For digital twin technology, this means that one could attempt to certify how the digital twin was created or certify the accuracy of the digital twin itself. Certification of a twin will be complicated by information overload. For example, most prescription drugs come with warnings about who can take them, disclaimers about negative side effects, and when to discontinue use. However, the vast amount of information known about a drug and the vaster amount of unknown information about a drug at time t will not be known until time t+1, and much of this vital information is only understandable by medical experts. The trust consideration for digital twin technology is how much information can be provided in a specific digital twin without overloading a user with extraneous information that leads to confusion about how to use the twin or what the twin even represents.

Propagation: One of the greatest trust concerns with any system of systems is how errors and corrupt data propagate during execution [38]. Digital twin technology experiences this trust consideration as well, particularly when different twins representing different physical objects are composed. This may suggest that a digital twin should be wrapped with pre-conditions and post-conditions to determine whether the output from one digital twin will be acceptable as input to another digital twin.

Counterfeiting: A digital twin could be tampered with or counterfeited, and there are schemes that could protect against this. For example, digital twin definitions could be hashed and the hash posted to a public web page, or users of a digital twin definition could hash their copy and compare it to the hash on the public web page. This said, web pages and other similar publicly accessible repositories can be hacked. To enhance trust, one could use a blockchain to publicly post a digital twin definition hash in an immutable data structure that could never be changed, even by malicious attackers. Alternatively, identical copies of a digital twin definitions and related instances could be stored in separate locations (e.g., in offline backups).

1. Introduction

A digital twin (DT) is an electronic representation of a real-world entity; providing the capability to evaluate this entity. A digital twin can emulate both physical things (e.g., buildings, electronics, living things), and non-physical things (e.g., processes, conceptual models). As with many new information technologies, digital twin technology employs existing foundational technologies and may reflect existing capabilities. It covers what currently exists in modeling and simulation but then casts a broader vision for future capabilities. The full benefits of digital twin technology will require interoperable definitions, tools, and standards as well as early consideration of digital twin cybersecurity and trust. This situation is especially true for nascent standards efforts that seek to define and structure the technology.

This report introduces the concept of a digital twin, describes the underlying technologies, and expands on its current capabilities by discussing key components, functions, and cybersecurity and trust considerations. It is not intended to define “digital twin” – this activity should be undertaken by SDOs. Any definition of “digital twin,” however, should address a set of technical considerations, which are offered herein. These technical considerations can also be used to test any definition that is created by any SDO.

Section 4 discusses typical operations performed on digital twins.

2. Definitions of Digital Twins

There are several existing definitions for digital twins. Some have been created by researchers, standards committees, consortia, and industry. Others are implicitly suggested by commercial enterprises that make statements about how their software applications are “digital twin-compliant.” Despite these definitions there is no agreed-upon definition for or consensus on the full potential of digital twins [1].
